Hi all,

I recently tested some oldish plates from Slavich, PFG-03M (expired early 2005). I dropped one straight into a JD-4 developer (no exposure) and it blackened almost immediately, is there any hope for these plates? The half empty box had been sitting around at room temp for about a year. I though somebody had mentioned you could salvage expired plates using reversal bleach, but I could not find the post.

posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.content_md:
> **John W:** Hi all,I recently tested some oldish plates from Slavich, PFG-03M (expired early 2005). I dropped one straight into a JD-4 developer (no exposure) and it blackened almost immediately, is there any hope for these plates? The half empty box had been sitting around at room temp for about a year. I though somebody had mentioned you could salvage expired plates using reversal bleach, but I could not find the post.

Hi John,

I think you may possibly have badly fogged plates for reasons quite different from normal photographic aging which with our ultra fine grain stuff means reduced photosensitivity (requiring a bit of aqueous TEA solution or vitramin C/sodium carbonate at pH 6-7 or even very dilute standard proprietary developer to reactivate them.) rather than chemical fogging. Somewhile ago many of us observed this fogging in Slavich plates and I have been told it was due to the wrapping paper they used which was giving off traces of formaldehyde. (I am sure this was discussed in Colin's earlier forum).

From experience with recovering fogged Agfa plates I found that 

20 grams of ferric EDTA salt with 10g pot bromide per litre worked to clear out the latent silver nuclei but the time spent in this very mild rehal bleach was important. Too short and it was still fogging and too long and grain growth started to spoil diffractive potential. What was essential though was that after washing out the bleach you needed to reactivate the plate with the solutions given in the above paragraph ie. mild reducing solution to compensate for the mildly oxidizing treatment you had to give it. I was amazed to find that the plates were then almost but not quite as good as new. (Don't try using dichromate for the oxidizing solution though, or the photosensitivity can remain zilch).

Jeff

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
It wouldn't be a reversal bleach, but a rehalogenating bleach. I discovered this by accident (and I am sure many others) by getting mixed up in the dark. Just use your favorite, PBQ, Fe EDTA, Copper Sulfate, etc, in the dark of course, a nice rinse, photo-flo, and dry in the dark. Don't use anything dichromate based, as it ruins the sensitizing dye.

More details in "Recycling Holographic Plates", Proceedings of the Third International Symposium on Display Holography, Lake Forest College, 1988.

Actually I see it also contains a simple idea for the laser users equivalent of a sundial with the shadow giving you the reference beam 

angle instead of the time of day. --A neat idea, it should be available to everyone.

I think since John W. described the fogging of the unexposed Slavich plates as going black in the dev. it sounds severe. So I think my suggested formula :

"20 grams of ferric EDTA salt with 10g pot bromide per litre "

Should be 40g ferric EDTA sodium salt and 20g KBr. Probably CuSO4 should be at the same level. (If you have the ferric EDTA compound it would be much more preferable I think because the vitally important sensitizing dyes might form copper complexes whereas the iron salt is already complexed up completely, there is also the possible formation of low refractive index Cu(1)Br particles) .

(A fascinating fact [to me] about both these oxidants that I discovered is that without any bromide ion present neither of them are strong enough to oxidize silver metal nuclei/grains. Pure quite concentrated solutions will not bleach your holograms if they are left in for a year and a day!

The reason for this must be that the energy that comes from the formation of the AgBr nano-crystals, 'lattice energy' is vital to tip the balance. ie. no net energy comes from forming soluble Ag

sulfate or the EDTA silver salt. Not even 10g potassium chloride instead of the bromide work OK I found because the AgCl is about 10 times more soluble than AgBr so lattice energy is lower. If you double or quadruple the Br level the bleaching rate goes up hugely , particularly with CuSO4)

Jeff

I wonder if an exposed and processed DCG plated can be recycled?

I imagine the reprocessed plate would have a thinner emulsion then the original starting plate.

So take a DCG hologram, put it in "hot" water with a concentration of AmDi. Dry, expose and process.

posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.content_md:
> **JohnFP:** Danny, I think you misunderstood what I said. Not reprocessing an existing hologram but taking a DCG hologram and make the emulsion such that it can be exposed again to make a different hologram.

An interesting idea of yours John. 

I never thought of it before but I would lay money (but not much) on the following plan working. Instead of damaging the gelatin as with strong alkali one just needs to just make the chromium binding break away and 

bind to something stronger leaving the gelatin pretty much intact chemically. So this can be done by soaking hologram in a strongish solution of EDTA disodium salt. (the tetrasodium salt would be too alkaline ). So its full name is ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid disodium salt , it is pretty harmless and available from many chemical suppliers.

Or you can get the free EDTA without sodium (used to be called sequesteric acid I think) and make it roughly neutral 

with sodium carbonate or something. 

But John what do you suppose will happen to those physical cracks that are induced during those desiccation steps? Even if they heal up they may

still remanifest themselves as weak points. - I dont know... I hope you or Danny will try it.

Jeff

> **DannyBruza:** yes i ve done that with old plate from dinesh using rosewater & glycerin.. making the plate close to new.. with a bit of noise

Sorry, I misundestood you. So you soaked in rosewater and glycerin then resensitized in a AmDi bath or there was AmDi right in the rosewater and glycerin? Also, what temperatures did you use?

Jeff, when I process DCG, I see two different drying methods physically on the emulsion. The first is what I believe to be the crack, as the entire emulsion develops very white opaque spider web like "cracks" that change into a very bright hologram and is usually a broader band replay. The second is a gradual color shift of the hologram to it's final color and non of the white "cracks" are ever seen. These are narrower band and seem to be less bright. The process may work for the latter of the two when making narrow band masters. 

I believe in the latter the crosslinking at the exposed sites contain a higher density of gelatin where as the unexposed regions get some of their gelatin washed away. If the plate was then un-crosslinked with a hot bath I believe the emulsion thickness would be dictated by the either the unexposed washed away thickness or the average of the exposed and unexposed thicknesses if the un-crosslinked areas would diffuse into the unexposed areas. Or would the surface relief between the two still remain.

One thing I did not know it DCG is not only a phase material but a surface relief material also. I think it was Dinesh that mentioned this. I always thought of it as being just a phase material.

Gosh knows I have plenty of "bad" holograms to play with. 

I will try some tests and report back.
